title: Fuel-Vapor Management — 5.0L 32V Ti-VCT
introduction: The 5.0L 32V Ti-VCT engine’s evaporative emissions system contains fuel vapor and sends it to the engine for later use. I read it as vapor traffic management: storage in the canister, a controlled route toward the intake and a separate connection to outside air. This overview explains those roles, without specifying physical hose routing, test values or repair steps.

edits.text: The evaporative emissions (EVAP) system keeps fuel-vapor hydrocarbons out of the atmosphere by storing the vapors and routing them to the engine, where they are consumed during normal engine operation.
edits.why: The system contains vapor for later use. Its role is distinct from the liquid-fuel delivery system, so a vapor-system fault alone does not identify a failed fuel pump.

edits.text: The EVAP system comprises the following storage, control, sensing and filler components:
edits.why: I use this inventory to keep the parts’ identities straight before reading more detailed system information.

edits.text: EVAP canister: the activated-carbon storage component that captures fuel vapor for later use by the engine.
edits.why: Purging removes stored vapor and prepares the carbon to capture more. The canister provides storage; the valves manage its flow paths.

edits.text: EVAP canister purge valve: the electrically controlled valve that meters vapor flow from the canister toward the engine intake.
edits.why: This valve manages the route through which stored vapor reaches the engine to be burned.

edits.text: EVAP canister vent solenoid: the electrically operated valve controlling the canister’s outside-air connection.
edits.why: The outside-air route serves a different purpose from the intake-bound purge route. Keep those valve identities distinct.

edits.text: Fuel Tank Pressure (FTP) sensor and tube: the system’s tank-pressure sensing components.
Easy Fuel (capless) fuel tank filler pipe: the capless entry used for refueling.
